# In Praise of Darkness

In the early morning hours of January 17, 1994, an earthquake measuring 6.7 rattled Los Angeles awake, cutting power across huge swaths of the city. In the strange quiet that followed, while residents checked on neighbors and worried about gas lines, local observatories reportedly began fielding unusual phone calls. People said there was something wrong with the sky. Something enormous and silvery had appeared overhead — a vast glowing smear where no such thing had ever been. Some feared the earthquake had caused it. Others wondered what else was coming.

What they were seeing was the Milky Way.

Generations of electric light had done their work so thoroughly that when the sky's default setting quietly returned over Los Angeles, many people didn't recognize it. They had lived entire lives beneath a dome scrubbed clean of its own galaxy, and nobody had mentioned the loss, because almost nobody remembered it being there. I think about those calls often. They read like one of the strangest records of modern life: human beings dialing emergency services in genuine alarm because they had glimpsed the universe.

We tend to file light pollution alongside noise pollution — an irritation, a quality-of-life complaint, a matter for zoning boards. But the loss cuts deeper than annoyance. A 2016 study in *Science Advances* found that more than 80 percent of North Americans can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. That isn't merely losing a pretty view. It's the erasure of the oldest shared experience our species has.

Consider what's actually up there. On a genuinely dark night, far from any city, a person with ordinary eyesight can spot a faint smudge high in the autumn sky: the Andromeda Galaxy, about two and a half million light-years away. It is the most distant object visible to the unaided eye. The photons landing on your retina tonight left Andromeda long before anatomically modern humans existed. Every naked-eye view of the night sky is time travel — not metaphorically, but literally, a direct receipt of ancient light. When we lose dark skies, we don't lose just stars. We lose the only portal we have through which the deep past arrives on its own, unmediated, requiring nothing but an upward glance.

Darkness, meanwhile, is not emptiness. Ecologically, it's infrastructure. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from nests at night and find the ocean by crawling toward the brighter horizon — moonlight and starlight glinting off water. Beachfront floodlights reverse that instinct catastrophically, sending thousands of hatchlings marching inland toward parking lots. Migrating birds navigate partly by the stars, a fact demonstrated elegantly in the 1960s when researchers showed that indigo buntings raised without access to the night sky could not orient properly. Insects spiral into fatal exhaustion around porch lamps. Fireflies conduct courtship in flashes calibrated against ambient darkness; brightened nights render their conversations unintelligible. Whole ecosystems run on schedules written in moonlight and starlight, and our glow is smudging the ink.

For nearly all of human history, the sky was the great shared text of our species. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean guided by star paths, memorized rising points of dozens of stars. Farmers across continents timed planting by the Pleiades. The Greeks called our galaxy *galaxias kyklos*, the milky circle, which the Romans rendered as Via Lactea — the milk spilled across heaven, a story older than either language. Perhaps most wonderful of all, the Inca looked into the dark lanes of the southern Milky Way — the shadows between stars — and found constellations there too: a celestial llama drinking from the river of the galaxy, a serpent, a toad. Imagine being so fluent in the night that even its negative space was legible, so intimate with the sky you could read its silences.

Against all this, the modern relationship feels impoverished. Most children today grow up learning about the Milky Way as an abstraction — a diagram in a textbook describing where we live — rather than as the luminous arch they could verify themselves by stepping outside. We know more about the universe than any generation in history and see less of it directly than any generation in history. That inversion seems worth mourning.

But here is the hopeful part: light pollution may be the only environmental catastrophe that disappears the instant you decide to stop causing it. Oil spills take decades to remediate. Carbon lingers for centuries. But flip a switch, shield a fixture, dim a sign after midnight — and the stars come back the same night. Since 1988, the International Dark-Sky Association has certified parks and reserves around the world where darkness is treated as a resource worth protecting, like clean water or old-growth forest. Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah became the first such park in 2007, its night skies so pristine that visitors routinely report the same stunned reaction as those Los Angeles callers in 1994. Municipalities have learned that fully shielded, warmer-colored lighting preserves safety while restoring the sky — the fixes are cheap, boring, and effective.

So consider this an invitation. Find the darkest patch of ground you can reasonably reach. Give your eyes half an hour to adjust — the chemistry of night vision is slow and easily ruined by one careless glance at a phone screen. Then look up. If conditions cooperate, you will see the pale river of your own galaxy arcing overhead, the light of hundreds of billions of suns, some of it older than every human who ever lived.

Those frightened callers in 1994 weren't really afraid of what they saw. I suspect they were feeling awe without having a name for it — the vertigo of encountering something vastly larger than themselves for the first time. That vertigo used to be a birthright, available to every human being on any clear night. It still is. The universe hasn't gone anywhere. It waits behind the glare, patient, broadcasting in ancient light, waiting for us to simply look up and remember what the room looks like with the skylight open.

**In Praise of Darkness**

At 4:31 in the morning on January 17, 1994, an earthquake measuring 6.7 struck Northridge, California, knocking out power across Los Angeles. In the hours that followed, while residents stumbled around darkened apartments checking on neighbors and water pipes, local observatories began receiving strange phone calls. People were frightened, they said. There was something enormous in the sky above their homes — a vast, glowing, silvery smear that hadn't been there before. Some suspected the earthquake had somehow caused it. Others wondered aloud whether it was a sign of something worse to come.

What they were seeing was the Milky Way.

Roughly a hundred years of electric light had done its work so thoroughly that when the sky's default setting reappeared over Los Angeles, thousands of people did not recognize it. They had grown up, driven cars, raised children beneath the glow of a sky scrubbed clean of its own galaxy, and no one had thought to mention what had gone missing, because no one alive remembered it being there.

I think about those phone calls often. They strike me as one of the strangest documents of modern life: human beings calling emergency services in alarm because they had glimpsed the universe.

We tend to talk about light pollution the way we talk about noise pollution — as an irritation, a quality-of-life issue, a matter for zoning boards. But the loss runs deeper than inconvenience. When you erase the night sky, you sever something old in us...

[continue]

Andromeda section: On truly dark nights, away from cities, a person with decent eyesight can see the Andromeda Galaxy, a faint smudge high in autumn skies. It sits about 2.5 million light-years from here, making it the farthest thing visible to the naked eye. Light that reaches your retina tonight left Andromeda before our genus existed. Looking up is time travel in only one direction — every glance at that smudge is a glance into deep time.

Ecology: Darkness isn't empty. For sea turtles, hatchling turtles emerge on beaches at night and find the sea by heading toward the brighter horizon — moonlight and starlight reflected off the water. Artificial light disorients them; they crawl inland toward streetlights and die. Migrating birds navigate using the stars. Insects spiral into fatal orbits around porch lamps. Whole food webs are keyed to lunar rhythms. An estimated billions of insects die annually at lights... (careful with numbers — studies estimate large numbers; I can say "billions" cautiously or just say staggering numbers). Fireflies signal with bioluminescent flashes tuned against ambient darkness; brightened nights make their courtship illegible.

History/culture: For nearly all human history the sky was the shared text of our species. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean reading star paths. Farmers planted by Pleiades rising. The Greeks called it galaxias kyklos, the milky circle; the Romans translated it as Via Lactea; both are translations of older ideas. The Inca looked at the dark patches within the Milky Way band and saw constellations there too — dark-cloud figures like a llama and a serpent. Even the shadows were named. Imagine a culture so fluent in the sky it could read the negative space.

Movement back: Since 1988, the International Dark-Sky Association has designated dark sky reserves/parks. Places like Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah became the first International Dark Sky Park (2007). Shielded fixtures, warmer bulbs, curfews — cheap fixes compared with most environmental problems. Light pollution is the rare pollutant that vanishes instantly when you flip a switch.

Closing: return to the phone calls — the fear those callers felt might be reframed as awe mislabeled. Something enormous appeared and they had no container for it. Invite reader to find darkness, let eyes adjust ~20-30 minutes, look up. The universe is still there, patient, broadcasting in light older than our species. We built a ceiling of glow and forgot the room had a skylight.

Para 8 (closing): ~140 words

- The anecdote: widely reported that people called 911 and observatories (Griffith Observatory) about a "giant silvery cloud" — the Milky Way. This story is commonly cited; it's been reported by astronomers including Ed Krupp of Griffith Observatory. Good enough to relate as a widely told account — I can phrase it as reported.
- 2016 Falchi et al. study in Science Advances: more than 80% of world population lives under light-polluted skies; ~one-third of humanity cannot see the Milky Way, including 60% of Europeans and nearly 80% of North Americans. Accurate.
- Andromeda distance: about 2.5 million light years. Correct.
- Genus Homo ~2.8 million years ago; Homo sapiens ~300,000 years. So Andromeda's light left before Homo sapiens existed — safe phrasing: "before anatomically modern humans walked the Earth." Actually 2.5 million years predates Homo sapiens (300k) comfortably. Good.
- Sea turtles: hatchlings orient toward brighter horizon; artificial lighting causes disorientation ("hatchling disorientation"). Correct.
- Birds: migratory birds use celestial cues including stars (Emlen's planetarium experiments with indigo buntings, 1960s). Correct.
- Dark constellations: Inca dark cloud constellations include Yacana (llama), Amaru (serpent), etc. Correct.
- Polynesian wayfinding: star compasses, star paths. Correct.
- IDA founded 1988 by David Crawford and Tim Hunter. First International Dark-Sky Park: Natural Bridges National Monument, Utah, 2007. Correct.
- Pleiades: agricultural calendars worldwide (e.g., heliacal rising of Pleiades marking planting seasons in many cultures, including Greek and Andean). Fine.

Word count target: ~1000. I'll write and estimate.

Format considerations: This should be prose — flowing paragraphs, possibly with a title. No headers needed beyond maybe a title. No bullet points. Length: user asked for 1000 words, so I should get close to that. I'll count as I draft mentally and adjust.

Let me write the final piece now.
